We were satisfied when we entered into confederation that we could sell our products in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, Quebec or Ontario, without having any tax imposed upon us, and I therefore say that it is extremely wrong that because these commercial travellers come down from the upper provinces to sell their goods in Prince Edward Island they should be taxed for the purpose of raising a revenue for that province. I say it is entirely wrong and from the beginning, although the hon. gentleman (Mr. Farqu-liarson) who has just spoken, is responsible in a large degree for the imposition of this tax, I have believed that it was unconstitutional. I do not think we can place a bar between provinces, one trading with the other. I think it is wrong and unconstitutional and I hope that the hon. Minister of Justice will, in the decision he is about to bring down, show that this tax on commercial travellers is an unconstitutional and wrong tax.

I think the statement that the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Kemp) so emphatically made that this Act is illegal is probably too strong. The propriety of the Act is one tiling, its legality is another thing, and this is just one of those questions upon which prominent lawyers have entertained differences of opinion. Whether the tax comes within the section of the British North America Act respecting taxation, or whether it is an interference with trade and commerce, is just one of those questions on which you might get a very distinguished lawyer from Toronto or Montreal to give you an opinion on either side, and one would have just as much chance of being right as the other. I am not justifying the tax upon its merits, but very distinguished members of the legal profession have held that the Act is entirely legal. That will ultimately have to be determined by the courts. I merely state that there are these two divergent opinions in regard to it.
Has the Justice Department here given any opinion ?
The Act has been allowed to go into operation. It has been deemed inexpedient to disallow it. Similar Acts I think have been in force in other provinces.
Is the work going on at Canoe Cove ?
Yes, it is going on now, and it will be completed in a short time. The vote for which we are now asking will complete the work.
Is it being done by contract or day labour ?

Tenders were asked and we received only

one, but it was so high that we could not j accept it and we went on by day labour, doing the work at a much cheaper rate. The work will be completed out of the vote that we are applying for, now.
In how many papers did the lion. Minister of Public Works publish an advertisement calling for tenders ?

I cannot say offhand, but we advertised in the usual way, in the papers we usually advertise in in the maritime provinces. I will give my hon. friend later on, if he wishes it, the names of the papers.

It is a most unusual thing in the province of Prince Edward Island, when you call for tenders for a public work, that you can only receive one tender, and I think that the hon. minister ought to be able to state how many papers he placed the advertisement in and during what time the notice was inserted in these papers. I see by looking in the Auditor General's Report that it cost $100 for this advertising, and I am confident that if the hon. gentleman had advertised in Prince Edward Island and made it known that this work was in contemplation, he would have received more than one tender. Under these circumstances the hon. gentleman ought to state all the facts in connection with this advertising.
I have no doubt that we advertised in the usual way.

I can justify the hon. Minister of Public Works in regard to the Canoe Cove Breakwater. He advertised twice and I saw the only tender that came in. It was unreasonably high. The work is being done by day's labour, and it is being done with great care. I think the work is necessary and that later on it will prove to be useful. Iam sorry that the hon. member for Prince (Mr. Hackett) is rather opposed to it.

I fully agree with the last suggestion in connection with the necessity of the work. It is a very necessary work. I know the locality very well, and 1 know the work is a very necessary one, but what I complain of is that the contractors of Prince Edward Island did not have a fair opportunity of tendering for this work. When the election was pending and when the hon. gentleman who formerly represented West Queen's, was about to be elevated to the Supreme Court bench, it was known that a vacancy would occur and the hon. gentleman who now represents that riding (Mr. Farquharson) has been using that work for the purpose of gaining support and carrying his election.
Cascumpec Harbour-closing opening through beach, $2,000.
What progress has been made in regard to this work ?
This work is located in the riding of my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett).
That is throwing money away.

Oh, no; only that the work, I am very much afraid, will involve a large expenditure of money. We have spent a pretty large amount of money there. The total expenditure to December last was $17,561.19. Now the total estimated cost of the proposed work is .$3,500. We want $1,500 more to complete the work. Instructions have been given to Mr. Egan to go on with the work, but as on some other occasions, he has not been able to do so. The work will be carried on in the ordinary way.

The minister has stated that $17,500 had been expended on Cascumpec harbour, but that is altogether apart from the present work. About three years ago, owing to freshets and high tides the sea broke through the sand hill separating Cascumpec bay from the gulf and allowed a great deal of water that should pass through the main channel to go through this inlet. It was necessary that the whole body of water should be concentrated on the main channel because the more water there is concentrated on a sand bar the better will become the channel. It was proposed three years ago in the estimates to take a vote to close up that inlet. That money has never been expended. At election time you will hear the Liberals standing on the platforms and saying that the government is spending a large sum of money for public works, but the people are humbugged, For three years this $2,000 have appeared in the estimates and not a dollar has been spent yet. Recently the Ottawa correspondent of the ' Charlottetown Patriot,' the government organ, telegraphed that $22,000 had been placed in the estimates for improving Cascumpec harbour. How is it that we have only $2,000 here now ? The Ottawa correspondent multiplied the vote by ten, and then added the $2,000 of the actual vote of last year, and so it was an easy thing for him to figure out the $22,000. What is the use of putting appropriations in the estimates unless you expend them. Do not endeavour to mislead the people like that. I trust that the minister will see that the $2,000 is now expended, and expended either under the supervision of a good foreman or let by open tender.

I find myself at times in very embarrassing positions. When I spend money my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) reproaches me with spending too much, and when I do not spend money he is mad at me. I have always endeavoured to be prudent. When the vote was first placed in the estimates I admit that I had not all the information that was required, but I have the information now,

and I can assure my hon. friend that the money will be judiciously expended. Does he object to the expenditure of that money ?
Mr. HACIvETT. Not at all.

If ' not at all ' then let the vote pass. I want the vote to go through in order to spend the money in the hon. gentleman's county. I cannot be accused of being a partisan because I am spending the money in the county of my hon. friend (Mr. Ilackett) and he is not a strong partisan of ours. I am doing the right thing by him and I hopd he will do the right thing by me and not ask any more questions.
Mr. HACIvETT. I do not find fault with the minister for expending this money because it is very necessary, but what I do complain of is that it should be put in the estimates and not expended.
Well, this time it will be expended.

All right.
Creosote! timber for general repairs to wharfs piers and breakwaters, $2,000.
Where is this creosote timber prepared ; I do not think it can be procured in this country.

I am very sorry that we are obliged to import this timber. We have contemplated for some time establishing a creosoting plant, but we have not done so. We may have been wrong in not doing so, but I would like to have an expression of opinion of the House on the subject.

The reason I am making the inquiry is that there has been a resolution passed recently by the Halifax Board of Trade suggesting that some encouragement might be given to the establishment of a plant for that purpose in one of the maritime provinces. I have not had an opportunity to investigate the subject at all, and I do not know if it would be practicable, but' it is the opinion of some of these gentlemen who have considered the subject, that the government should see whether or not it would be in the interest of the country to give encouragement to such an establishment in Canada. Of course, I suppose it would depend very much on the cost of the plant which the minister says would be $35,000 or $40,000. These gentlemen seem to think they have facilities to do the work there, and it is a matter that should have the attention of the government. I know there is a great deal of this timber used in public works around the province of Hon. Mr. TARTE.
Nova Scotia. It is rendered necessary as I understand by the presence of worms in some of the harbours which destroy in a very few years timber that is not treated in this way ; whereas creosoted timber is impervious to the attacks of worms for a very considerable period. Could the hon. gentleman give us an idea of how much of this timber is used in the public works of Canada in the course of the year.

There is a great deal in what my hon. friend (Mr. Borden, Halifax) says. The question has been discussed several times since I have been in office here. Timber of this kind to the value of about $70,000 is used in the Public Works Department. If we had a plant, more than timber would be used. For instance, creosoted railway ties last longer.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax. Is that quantity used by the Public Works Department alone ?
Yes.
There is some used in the construction of piles for railway bridges and possibly there is some used in the other departments of the government.
Yes.
If the minister could tell us how much of this timber is used altogether in the public service of Canada, it might be useful information to those gentlemen who propose to engage in this business.

I cannot sqy how much is used altogether. Speaking for myself, I think we should have an establishment of that kind. There is a large work at Cape Tormentine that has been destroyed because it has been built with timber that was not creosoted. It is a question of money again, but since the leader of the opposition has called my attention to the question, perhaps I will ask my colleagues to look more carefully into the matter when the supplementary estimates are discussed. It is a very important question.

What these gentlemen had apparently in mind was the establishment of some such plant by private enterprise. What the minister seems to have in mind is the establishment of a plant under a department of the government. The advantage of doing it by way of private enterprise of course would be that a supply in that case would be available for private operations throughout the country. I suppose that more or less of this timber is used outside of the requirements of the government.
I do not think so.
There is a considerable quantity used.

I would suppose that people who construct wharfs aud works of that kind in the maritime provinces would require some of it. Perhaps the hon. gentleman from Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall would know as to this.
If such a plant be established by private enterprise I would make it my duty to buy in Canada, every piece of creosoted timber that we would want. I would only he too glad to do so.

Hear, hear,
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) There is not a wharf or breakwater that has been built but that a large quantity of this timber is used. Perhaps the largest wharf in the Dominion is now being built at Sydney by the Nova Scotia Steel Company, and they have imported a whole steamer load of this timber, but it will not be sufficient for them. The only place that this pine can be prepared successfully in the Dominion of Canada, would be, I think, around Quebec, because I do not think that we have the quality and quantity of pine in Nova Scotia that would be sufficiently large for the requirements of timber prepared in this manner. I think the subject is well worthy of the consideration of the Minister of Public Works and the other members of the government as to whether we shall not prepare this timber in our own country.

Hear, hear.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) It would not only be used by the government but by other people who are building wharfs and other works in connection with shipping.
Souris, Knight's Point-strengthening of breakwater, &c., $20,000.

Under contract.
Summerside Harbour-breakwater, $35,000.
Under contract ; the work going on.

I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works what progress is being made with this breakwater. I understood that it was to be completed last year, and I further understand that the plans are not workable, and that in consequence the contractors are having a great deal of difficulty in the construction of the breakwater. I would like to know what is being done, and when the breakwater is likely to be completed ?

The plans are all right aud workable. The
contractors, Messrs. McDonald & Moffat, of Sydney, have not, however, made the progress we hoped they would make. They *may be a little slow, but still I feel that they could carry on the work with more activity than they have displayed. We have notified them that they must go on with their work.
Have you any idea when this breakwater will be completed ?

The chief engineer tells me that if the contractors apply the energy they should apply, the work can be completed in one year. Now, these gentlemen must go on with their work. If they do not do so, we might have to have recourse to urgency measures. We might have to take the work from them.
Committee.

Secretary.
This document, I believe, was accompanied by a largely signed petition-some 800 signatures, including the names of some of the most influential men in Queen's and Prince counties. The petitioners state that as the Cape Traverse branch of the Prince Edward Island Railway runs through a populous country and serves a prosperous people, the purposes of the railway are to a great extent nullified by the fact that there are no terminal facilities. It is true, a wharf was built at Cape Traverse at considerable expense ; but unfortunately it was put at the wrong place, and for the last few years practically no work has been done on it, except for a week or so before the last election, and the work was stopped a day after the election. However, the best authorities there are of opinion that a suitable place for the construction of a wharf can be had near Cape Traverse, along by Carleton Point, and this petition asks that the minister place a sufficient sum in the supplementary estimates to guarantee this work going on. I think that the Minister of Marine and Fisheries understands that this is the most natural route for steamers in both winter and summer, because they have not the difficulties to overcome that are encountered in going to Georgetown. The distance across the channel to Cape Tormentine is only 8 miles ; but from the nature of the ice on the New Brunswick side, it is almost impossible for a steamer to land, especially in the condition in which the pier is now. The idea of the petitioners is that a suitable wharf should be built at Cape Traverse, for both summer and winter navigation and that a fery should be established there. A great Mr. LEFURGEY.
deal of produce has to be brought down the line to Charlottetown or Summerside to be shipped across, and if the facilities were provided which were contemplated when the Cape Traverse branch was built, there would be a vast improvement in the trade of that section. The minister has no doubt received and considered this memorial, and I would like to have some word from him as to what he intends to do about granting the prayer of this petition by placing a vote in the supplementary estimates.

The hon. gentleman is asking me, if I understand him correctly, to place in the supplementary estimates an amount of money to provide accommodation at Cape Traverse, I remember receiving a petition to that effect. My hon. friend has spoken of elections. It is very seldom that we do not hear that word elections in connection with any work on Prince Edward Island. What are the facts ? Under the late administration there was about $275,000 spent at Cape Tormentine. That is a large amount of money. The work was built with improper materials, and with timber which was not creosoted. Twelve months after the work was completed it was destroyed. I suppose it was not an election work ; it was not a very good work, at any rate. At Cape Traverse there was another work built under the late regime. I do not recriminate ; I simply state the facts. There has been about $40,000 spent at Cape Traverse on a wharf which my hon. friend has just said was badly located. Now he wants me to put in the supplementary estimates an amount of money to provide accommodation elsewhere. I would like very much to have his views as to the location of the works in the maritime provinces.
Iam informed that the steamer ' Stanley ' has been trying to do the service during the whole winter of Prince Edward Island and Nova Scotia, but has not worked very well. This very work at Summerside, on which we have embarked, is intended to provide accommodation for that winter service. We are doing our best, and cannot experiment in two or three places at the same time. We cannot carry out experimental work right and left in that way. I would be very glad to do all I can for that interesting island, but we have to spend a pretty large amount on that winter service, and must know exactly where we are before incuring further expenditure.
Two wrongs do not make a right, and the fact that mistakes have been made-

Hon. members perhaps do not quite understand how the island is situated with regard to this matter. We are separated from the Nova Scotia shore by about eight miles of water. On the Cape Tormentine side a large amount of

money lias been spent, and It will be necessary to spend more money to complete the work there. On the Cape Traverse side little or nothing has been done. There is no ferry at this crossing but railways on either side and at either terminus. To go to the capital by water from Pictou over the route now followed, or from Cape Tormeutine, is a distance of forty or forty-five miles, and the hon. minister will understand how willing we are to have that reduced to eight miles. Many people, especially tourists, do not want to cross so much water, as the crossing is very rough particularly in the fall, and we are anxious to have distance reduced. I am in sympathy with what the hon. member (Mr. Hackett) has said. I believe that in the near future our government must see its way Clear to place an amount in the estimates in order to provide for summer and winter ferry at that point. That is absolutely necessary, and when other provinces are receiving benefits which are denied our little province, we have a right to insist on that being done and to combine in forcing our claim on the government, no matter how we may differ in local matters. I am satisfied that in a few years there will be a ferry traversing that eight miles, and thus save the forty miles travel which at present has to be undertaken. Why should we go forty miles when we can shorten the distance to eight, and when there is railway accommodation on either side. We are asking for a wharf at Cape Traverse. Perhaps the hon. minister may not see his way clear to give it to us this session, but it will have to come in the near future no matter what government is in power.

I am very thankful for the information given me and will give more attention than ever to this important question. If it be true, as I hope it is, that communication between the island and the mainland can be shortened to eight miles, there is no government which can refuse to undertake that work, but there must be some obstacle in the way or it would have been done long ago. However, we are in a century of progress, and I will give my best attention to the statements just made. I will have my officers go again into that important question, and if it can be done, I will pledge myself to do it.	.

I am very much pleased indeed to hear the statement of the hon. minister because I know that when he makes a promise of that kind he means to keep it. I believe It will not be very long before government works are constructed at Carleton Point, Prince county, for the purpose of maintaining winter and summer communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. I do not want to minimize what the hon. gentleman has done with regard to public works in the
island, but to impress upon him the necessity of completing the work he has begun.
We may disagree, and we may say things that are pretty sharp sometimes. But I want to say that when the hon. gentleman tells us that he will do a thing, he will do it. Yesterday, in the discussions in this House we had a gale blowing from the prairies of the North-west; this evening we have a breeze from the east, from the province of Prince Edward Island. I am pleased indeed to find that the hon. minister is paying so much attention to our remarks. We are a small province, but we claim that we are as intelligent and as bright as any people in the Dominion of Canada. We are only asking for our rights as guaranteed us by the terms of confederation. Now, you have two steamships running to keep up communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland. They run at times for forty or fifty miles in floating ice. If the government will construct a pier at Carleton Point, it would make it possible to keep up that communication. I trust the hon. minister, if he can not see his way clear at the present time to construct this pier, will keep it in view as his ultimate object. By this means the service will be kept up from Cape Tormentine to Cape Traverse, running to Carleton Point, winter and summer. In that way, you will solve the problem of winter communication and satisfy the people of Prince Edward Island. I am glad that the hon. member for West Queen's (Mr. Farquharson) has, in almost his maiden effort, in this House raised his voice in favour of this route. We call upon him to continue to support us in this matter.
Public Works-chargeable to income-harbours and rivers-New Brunswick-Bay du Vin- to complete reconstruction of wharf, $4,000.
Has the contract for this work been let ?
Yes, the contract was let, on the 27th of May, 1901, to Mr. Charles Ransborough.
I find certain charges respecting this work noted at page V-172 of the Auditor General's Report. Have these charges been incurred since the contract was given ?
The chief engineer informs me that certain repairs were done outside of the contract, and it may be to these that my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) refers.
What is the amount of the contract ?
The amount is $7,745.

Referring to page V-172, of the Auditor General's Report, I see that the last items referred in this Bay du

Vin work are $31.31 for the King's Printer and $140.81 for advertising, making a total of $178.15. What do these two items of King's Printer and advertising refer to ?

I understand that they refer to the printing and advertising the specifications.
Black Brook (Logieville)-wharf, $1,000.

That is under contract.
Cape Tormentine-repairs to breakwater, &c., $15,000.
There should be some explanation of so large an item as this.

I have already said-perhaps my hon. friend was not in the House-that this work has cost a large amount of money. Unfortunately, material was used in the construction of this wharf, years ago, that should not have been used. Creosoted timber was not employed as it should have been. Now, we have to rebuild the work using rip rap to keep it from falling to pieces. We seek in this way to save a large work which has cost a great deal of money and which we hope will be used as one of the piers in connection with the winter service between New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island.

Could not the hon. gentleman give us some idea what portion of this vote is for material and what portion is for labour 7 There should be some ex-jdanation beyond the mere statement the hon. minister has given.
Superintendence will cost about $1,500. The balance will be spent in buying material. We are simply buying big stone and rip-raping the whole work.

I am not going to criticise this vote, as I know how necessary the work proposed is. But I would like to call the attention of the hon. minister to the need for dredging along the outside of the pier in order that the winter boats may come up alongside the wharf. Is it the hon. minister's intention to do that work also ?
The .^xNISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. I have tried in vain to get a dredge for this and other works. Unfortunately, in the maritime provinces, we are short of dredges. We should have some dredging done there in order to allow the steamer to come alongside the pier. I understand every word the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) has said.
Caraquet-wharf, $20,000.	[DOT]
We would like some explanation of this.
That work is practically under contract now.

We have asked for tenders, and have accepted the tender of Simmons & Burpee as the lowest. That work is of great importance. I may say that since it became known that we were going to do this work at that point, several lumber industries have been established there.
Is the land on which this wharf is to be erected the property of the government or of private individuals ?
The engineer informs me we have not bought any land yet, but the work is on land belonging to the government.
Who owns the land at the inland end of the wharf ?

I am thankful for the suggestion of my hon. friend. I have given most positive instructions to all my officers not to begin any work without having made arrangements with the owners of the land. There is an understanding about the land, but not in writing. I will say that before doing anything further I will see that we get a deed of the land, because we have trouble every time unless that is done. In this case, however, I do not think there is going to be any trouble.
Is the site located yet ?
Yes, the work is located, but there will not be any trouble about the land, because the work is just on the shore.
The minister says there have been some verbal negotiations going on; what is the price ?
1 understand the price is about $20 for the right of landing there. I suppose the insignificance of the price is the reason why a written deed has not been made.
Perhaps the price will be raised now that the site is taken. [DOT]
Before the contract is awarded I will see that the deed is in my hands. A tender has been accepted, but the contract has not been signed.
Who is the owner of the land ?

Mr. James Blackball.
Chance harbour-breakwater, $4,000.
I move that that item be struck out.
I notice in the Auditor General's Report that $190 have been expended on that for advertising. Why advertise if it was not intended to build ?
We have since found out that the work was too expensive to do this year.
Then the $190 is lost.
Not lost, because it has given us information that will be useful later on.
Could not that same information have been obtained without the expense of advertising ?
Perhaps so. But it is better to have that item struck out, that work would cost about $40,000.

Motion agreed to.
Dipper harbour-breakwater, $3,250.
I move that that item be struck out.

We find another advertising bill here for $224.44 in connection with this. In looking over these advertising accounts it seems to me that they run a little irregularly. The other night the Minister of Public Works said that he had advertised for building that breakwater down near Wilson's Beach. I am not surprised when I look over this list that he did not get any tenders. I regret that the Grit papers in our county were not better paid for advertising. I see in this Wilson's Beach matter, which will be a work costing from $25,000 to $35,000, he only paid $04.70 for advertising. Now, both these items are struck out after advertising for tenders. We also find some that run higher than that. It is evident the minister was not very anxious to have Wilson's Beach breakwater let by tender, or he would have put it in the hands of other newspapers so that it would have been more thoroughly advertised.

Motion agreed to.
Grand© Anse-extension and repairs to breakwater, $9,000.
There was a lot of expenditure in connection with Grande Anse last year. Is this the same breakwater ?
It is the same breakwater. This year we are only taking a revote to complete the work.	,
But this work is evidently done by day's work.

Motion agreed to.
Point Wolfe-breakwater, $2,000.

Who has charge there ? Who located it ? As I understand it at Point Wolfe there has been considerable money expended and parties who live in the vicinity say that some of it has not been very well expended. They claim that the fault lies with the engineer in not knowing exactly what he was about. I suppose the 33
money is being expended under the direction of Mr. Shewen, who is the engineer of the department in that locality ?
Yes.

I should like to know whether the hon. minister has ascertained the views of the people in that neighbourhood who are well acquainted with the tides and the movements of the currents there and who know just where this breakwater should be located.

I do not now remember that we have received any complaints as to the manner in which the work has been carried out.
It was carried out under Mr. Shewen's supervision. I would be very glad to receive any information at the hands of my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler) if he thinks something was done that should not have been done.

There have been complaints as to the Point Wolfe and Alma expenditure, more particularly in regard to the Alma expenditure.
Richibucto-reconstruction of north pier and groynes, &c., $20,300.

I would like some information as to this Richibucto matter. This seems a very large vote. I notice the hon. member for Kent (Mr. LeBlanc) in his place and perhaps he may have some information upon the subject.

That is an old work that has cost a large amount of money, and it was in a very bad state of repair. I visited the place a couple of years ago. The work was simply in the worst possible state. We started repairing the work by day's labour. We had a good deal of trouble and I finally made up my mind that the best way of ending my worry was to ask for tenders. We have done so. The tenders are in, but I have not had time as yet to pronounce upon them. The work will be given to the lowest tenderer if there, is nothing to prevent me from doing so.
I see that you spent nearly $17,000 last year. Is this vote in addition to that ?
Yes.
That will be about $37,000.

The work has cost a large amount of money. The original work that we are repairing to-day cost about $150,000. My hon. friend knows the amount of work there is to do. It is a long pier that forms the entrance to the bay. It is a necessary work.

While we are at these estimates, I would like to call the attention



of the hon. minister to the fact that there is a great variation in the prices of lumber supplied at these different works. I notice here, page V-173, Auditor General's Report, in connection with the repairs to the breakwater at Campobello (Wilson's Beach) that in some cases hemlock is charged for at $11 a thousand which would be a fair price. This is one of our cheapest woods, but I find that in another place another contractor charged for hemlock $19.50 a thousand.
An lion. MEMBER. The same work ?
It is the same work but not the same man.
Not on the same day and not from the same place either.

There has never been in the history of the lumber business, as far as I am acquainted with it, and I think I know something about it, such a variation in the price as that during the same season, or in fact any season-a difference of $8.50 a thousand. I see that Messrs. John Dewar & Sons supplied hemlock at $11 a thousand and that for the same work Mr. F. E. Sayre supplied hemlock at $19.50 a thousand, and birch hewn timber at $17.50 a thousand.

I know my hon. friend does not want to be unfair, but he has only to look at the statement and lie will see that it is not the same kind of timber at all. There is sawn timber, log timber and hewn timber, and these are not the same classes of timber at all. It may be hemlock, but it is hemlock prepared in a different way. I may say that my officers have received and are receiving the most positive instructions to buy material at the lowest possible prices in the market, and I do not think that any member of parliament will be able to prove before the Public Accounts Committee that I have done anything other than that. My officers are always instructed to buy material at the lowest possible prices, and on this occasion the hon. gentleman will find that this is not the same material at all.

No, it should be cheaper in the one case than in the other. The smaller the size a log is cut into and the more sawing you do the higher the price will be. But here, this timber is simply squared. Hewn hemlock was charged for at the rate of $17.50 a thousand by Mr. Sayre and the other at $19.50 a thousand while the other man sells his timber at $11 a thousand.
That is round timber.
Supposing that is the ease, it is altogether too high a price. Seven

dollars would be a good price for hemlock round. It is only a question of towage. Suppose you towed it from the mouth of the St. John river it would not cost more than $1.25 a thousand, and here is a charge besides for towage in Mr. Sayre's bill.
I am informed that the timber came from the county of Albert.

No, that timber came from up the River St. John. That is where Mr. Sayre's timber lands are located. He is a merchant living in the city of St. John. This timber would come down the St. John river, either from Mr. Sayre's own lands on the Salmon river, a tributary of the St. John, or from the lands on the upper waters of the St. John river. If it were squared timber, it certainly should not cost as much as boards, and the very highest price of hemlock boards is $9 a thousand. Here we have a charge of $17.50 a thousand. That is from $0 to $7 a thousand out of the way.

If my hon. friend is right, my officers are wrong, and on the other hand, if my officers are right my hon. friend is wrong. It is all very well to state on the floor of parliament that the price of this and that article is too high. Conditions are not always the same. In New Brunswick I have had at times some little trouble here and there, but I have never found that any extraordinary charge has been made. However, my chief engineer will take a note of what my hon. friend says and inquire as to the reason why there is that difference. I understand that the timber is long timber, specially long, 45 feet long. It is pretty difficult to judge of these matters on the floor of the House. It is easier to speak than to buy cheaply.

Hemlock grows very tall in our country, and it is the cheapest lumber we have in our country. Therefore, it is no excuse or argument to say that it is long timber, beca'use long timber would be nearly as cheap as short timber. It sells by the thousand feet and there is no argument in that. I may say, no matter how much confidence the hon. minister may have in his officers, that they are clearly wrong in this instance. This man has received from $6 to $7 a thousand too much for his lumber, and I am giving you the benefit of the doubts.

I would be very sorry to And out that my hon. friend is right. I will find out tomorrow whether he is right or wrong. I have discovered no information that has come to me on that point. I will find out the reason for the price he paid. If my hon. friend is wrong, I will ask him to say that he is wrong.
I will be very glad to do so.
Well, I will make that bargain with him.
I am quite agreeable, but I shall expect that my hon. friend will be reciprocal and will acknowledge it if he is wrong.

My chief engineer is instructed to wire to Mr. Shewen to know why he has paid that price, because his hands have always been free. He, like all my other officers, are ordered to buy at the lowest market price.
I challenge any member of parliament on either side to say that I have given any other order than that. Mr. Shewen will be wired immediately and I will communicate the answer to my hon. friend (Mr. Fowler). That is fair, I suppose.

Not exactly fair and for this reason :	That you are wiring to get
your information from the same man who made the mistake, which I do not think is fair at all. It is not necessary for the minister to get heated over the matter because I am not imputing the slightest blame directly to him. I only say that his officers have deceived him in this matter, as his friend deceived him the other day about the appointment of a clerk of works at the Sussex armoury. I do say that there are gentlemen supporting the minister on the other side of the House who know something about the price of lumber in the province from which we come, and if they state what they know to be the fact, they will state that this is an excessive price for any hemlock lumber ; and not only for hemlock, but he has charged $17.50 a thousand for birch, which is a very high price. The ordinary rough pine and not clear pine would be used for the purpose of a breakwater. If this were clear pine the price would not be excessive, but for the class of pine that would go into a breakwater it is an excessive price-that pine is worth $7 or $8 a thousand.
If Mr. Shewen paid too much I would be surprised because he is one of the hardest men I have met in my life.
Then get your information from another source than Mr. Shewen and you will be surprised.

I will ask my officer why he paid that much and from whom he asked quotations, because I am sure he did ask for quotations. If my hon. friend gives me any other source of information I am prepared to accept it. I do not desire to shield any one of my officers. I cannot be held responsible directly if too high prices are paid, but I am always anxious to get information.
33i

If the minister will communicate with his officer and get the reasons that his officer gives for these high prices, then if these reasons do not appear satisfactory to me I will give him the names of persons with whom he can communicate, and who are experts in the lumber business.

I will be very glad to receive the information.
River St. John, including tributaries, $16,000.
How does the minister propose to spend that appropriation of $16,000.

We have not yet decided on the work to be done. Last year we spent very little of that appropriation. There are works of several kinds to be carried out there. We have works at Oromocto, at Tobique, at St. Francis, at Bear Island and at Topaz. This vote is for clearing the river generally. It is a very changeable river as the hon. gentleman knows and it contains snags and sandbars of all kinds, so that it is very difficult to name the particular places at which the work will be caried on.

I am very well acquainted with the river and I know where the works have been carried out. I would urge on the attention of the minister the importance of making an effort to dear that channel. Last year, under the direction of Mr. Shewen, the resident engineer, dredging was commenced where the water was sufficiently deep, and quite unnecessary work was carried on for some time.
At what place ?

At Oromocto. There was a good deal of criticism on the work, and it was said that the engineer was not going about it properly. He should have commenced directly on the shoal. At a period when the water was at a proper depth the work could have been carried on properly. At all events they had to discontinue the work which they commenced. I would urge upon the minister the necessity of directing his attention to that particular point on the river, namely the Oromocto shoals.
River St. John-wharf at Oromocto, $1,500.
Does the minister propose to make any other appropriation for that wharf ?

-It was represented to me that the work would cost a large amount of money and then I paused. Later on we had another estimate based on a new survey and we found the work would cost $6,000. We are now preparing plans and asking for tenders for that work.
The work will be gone on with ?

Yes.
St. John harbour-Negro Point breakwater,
What is being done there?

That work has cost a large amount of money, but the waves are so big there that every year we are obliged to make repairs. This vote is to lay down large blocks of concrete to complete the work.
Upper Salmon river (Alma Pier), $5,700.
Will this work be let by contract ?

Yes, we have asked for tenders but the contract has not yet been awarded.
Grande Vallee-pier, $25,000.
I would like to know something about that $25,000 for a pier at Grande Yallee. What business is there, to warrant this expenditure ?

There are large lumber operations carried on In that part of the country, and it was to help that trade that the money was voted last year. The contract for the work has been awarded and I am simply asking parliament to give me the money to pay for that contract which wras commenced on the vote of last year.

That is just the understanding I have in regard to this matter- that the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) owns large timber properties in that section 'of the country, and that this wharf is virtually being built in the interest of a lumber company in which that hon. gentleman is largely interested-that it is wholly an electioneering matter.

The hon. gentleman has not been elected there ; he has been elected elsewhere, where he will be elected again. So this is not an electioneering work, The money for this work was voted last year, and it is being voted again this year, and it is rather late for the hon. gentleman to object to that work now.
I have had information that that is the sole purpose of this pier- to make the lumber property of the hon. member for Stanstead valuable. What is the population of the locality ?

I have just stated that the work has been undertaken in view of large lumbering operations-not because there is a town there ; and I may add that there is no other harbour on the north shore. So that the wharf will Hon. Mr. TARTE.
be used for lumbering operations, for trade purposes, and for shelter for the fishermen.

It is a most excellent advertisement for any man who has a good lumber property. AH he has to do, if he votes right, is to come to this government and ask for an appropriation to increase the value of his lumber property. Will the hon. minister tell us whether the site for this pier has been purchased and paid for, and if so, from whom ?

It has not. The fact that the hon. gentleman who represents Stanstead may have property there is no reason why the government should not make any improvements. My hon. friend from Charlotte (Mr. Ganong) has large properties in his riding, and I am carrying out improvements there. My hon. friend will not be accused of serving his own interests when he is insisting on money being spent in his riding. This is no argument.
Not if the money is spent for general purposes ; but when it is spent for the special purpose of increasing the value of a lumber property, I claim it is wrong.

There is no doubt that any public works improve the value of property, and if a member of parliament happens to have property in a place where these works are going on, so much the better for him. It does not injure the county.
Will the hon. minister be kind enough to tell us from whom the site was purchased and the price ?
There has been no land purchased. The wharf is built on the shore.
It must front on some one's land.

This seems to be an extraordinary proposition. From what has dropped, it would appear that there is a saw-mill situated at this place, and unfortunately there is no proper dock for a large lumbering business. The minister asks the House to vote this large sum for the construction of this dock, and he cannot tell whether a site has been purchased, or if so what the price of the site is. Before the item goes through, I think the minister should state the population of the place, whether the municipality is giving the land lot and the water lot adjoining, and whether there is any contribution by the municipality towards the construction of the dock.

The municipality has not given any contribution-not more than the municipality of Midland will give us, I suppose, for works

which we will build there. This dock is being built in the province of Quebec under the ordinary rules which are applied in all the provinces. No site has been purchased, because it was not necessary to purchase a site. An amount was voted in the estimates last year for this work ; I have been notified to go on with it, and. it is rather late now for hon. gentlemen to complain that we are going on because my hon. friend has property there, hon. gentlemen opposite begrudge the expenditure of the money. I do not think it is fair. The work is being built on a rocky point that does not belong to anybody.
It must belong to somebody. It is Crown land ?
I suppose it is Crown lands.
Is the work commenced ?
Oh, yes. I am simply asking for a vote to supplement the vote of last year. The contract is let, and the work is going on.
How much was voted last year ?
Last year I had a vote of $15,000. I have been fully authorized to go on with the work.
If this work was going to cost $40,000, how is it you had only an estimate of $15,000 last year ?
My department asks each year for the amount we expect will be spent during the year, and afterwards we ask what is necessary to supplement the vote.
What was your engineer's estimate of the whole cost of the work ?
The amount of the contract is $53,000.
And this work is begun without your having any title to the land on which it is built.
Because it is not necessary to have one. The work is built in the water.
It must be built on land.
It is built on a rocky point which belongs to the Crown.

It does not matter whether it is a rock or not. It must belong to a private party or to the Crown. If it belongs to the Crown, it belongs, I suppose, to the province of Quebec. The minister, it seems to me, has placed himself in a very peculiar position. He is spending $53,000 on property to which he has no title whatever. What sort of an arrangement can vou make if this property really belongs to
a private individual ? If it belongs to the gentleman who owns these vast lumber lands in that district, you should have got a deed from him before you began the improvements.
In this case it was not necessary to buy the site because the work is built on a point which does not seem to belong to anybody unless to the Crown.
Is it all wilderness there ?
There is a good deal of wilderness there.
Is there not a village or town or any inhabitants ?
There is a small village.
About what is the population ? It has a very elaborate name.
According to the last reports, the population was 370.
What are the industries ?
Lumber and fishing.
Is there a saw-mill there ?
Yes.
How many hands does it employ ?
I cannot say.
Perhaps the hon. Minister of Agriculture, who looks after the census, can tell ?

The strength of the Minister of Public Works is certainly shown in the vote now being taken. He presumes so much on his followers that he lets a contract for $53,000 for the construction of a dock, for which he only asked an appropriation of $15,000, and relies on his followers to support him in making the balance of the grant good.
And they will.

What is the position ? The hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) owns a saw-mill at this point, and taking advantage of his position as a supporter of the government, applied to the Minister of Public Works to have a dock constructed there for the purpose of carrying on his own business. This is on all fours with the vote last year of $75,000 for the construction of a dock at Depot Harbour for the sole benefit of Mr. Booth. The hon. minister last year made a present of $75,000 worth of dockage to Mr. Booth, which that gentleman is today about to dispose of to another corporation. In other words, we increased the value of Mr. Booth's assets to the tune of

$75,000, and the minister did this, knowing that his followers would blindly vote it through. Surely there must be some hon. gentlemen on that side, who, if they feel no moral responsibility themselves, must feel that they are responsible to the people who sent them here. Will they not protest against expenditures of this kind ? I submit that the hon. minister had no right to enter into a contract for $53,000 until he had got the assent of the House. I do not recall last year's vote on this particular question, but 1 believe that a reference to ' Hansard ' will not prove that the hon. minister stated then that there would be an expenditure of $53,000. If the rule is to be laid down that any hon. gentleman who has the requisite l>olitical leverage can have his own private property improved at the expense of the country, it would be well that the country should know it at once. I must congratulate the Minister of Public Works on this fact, that he has not the slightest fear that his followers will not vote through any appropriation he chooses to bring down. This is another tribute to the strong position he holds in the cabinet.

Let me say to my hon. friend that I am not alone in this government and that no contract of this kind can be carried out unless it is approved by my colleagues. I stand here responsible for what I have done just as I am for what they do, and just as they are for what both they and I have done.
I am very much surprised that some of my friends in the other provinces, where much larger works have been carried out, find so much fault- with a work of this kind carried on elsewhere. I gave the House the figures the other day to show that in Ontario there has been a large amount of money expended. In Southampton, for instance, there has been spent a quarter of a million dollars, and I make bold to say that in a few years there will be as much trade in this Grand Vallee a.s there is in Southampton. I admit that it is a pretty large amount to expend but I did not deceive the House. Last year, if my hon. friend had asked me how much the work would cost, I would have told him. The House granted me '$15,000 to build the work and it is now under contract. Do hon. gentlemen want me to repudiate my obligations ? I have never entered into any contract without their consent. I have not deceived anybody. My colleagues know perfectly well what I have done. I can sign no contract, and have no desire to do so, without going before my colleagues. But because the hon. member for Stanstead (Mr. Lovell) has mills in that vicinity, my hon. friend raises a row. I cannot help that. The work has to be paid for because the contract is signed, and no doubt it will prove a very useful work.

The point I make is this, that the vote is not for a work of public Mr. BENNETT.
utility, but solely in favour of a private interest, namely, a saw-mill owned by the hon. member for Stanstead. Let the expenditure be large or small, the question for us is whether it is for the public utility or simply for the benefit of one private individual. The hon. minister referred to grants in Ontario. Well, in the riding I have the honour to represent I was pleased to see that he has made grants. But under what circumstances ? At the town of Midland there are large industries and a good harbour, and if by the receding of the water, the elevators cannot be approached, is it not the bounden duty of the government to step in and do the necessary dredging ?
And we did it.

But if the hon. minister were asked to make a grant for the benefit of any saw-mill owner in East Simcoe-as he has done in this matter-I should object to that expenditure, whether it were in my riding or not. I have objected to expenditures made by the hon. gentleman in my riding. I objected notably to the construction of a dock at a village called Ilawkes-tone. I do not hold the minister accountable for all these expenditures, because his colleagues are equally culpable; and in the case of the dock at Hawkestone, the recommendation came from the Postmaster General. But I can tell the hon. minister that I look with pleasure on expenditures such as are made at Hawkestone. for this reason, that they show the people how the publie money is being frittered away in the attempt to make some petty political capital. But this expenditure recoils on the hon. gentleman. The whole thing was a political job. The man in charge of the work was a hotel-keeper, who lived a mile or so away, and was charging three dollars a day for superintending the work. The question is not whether the expenditure is large or small, but whether it is simply aiding the promotion of a private enterprise, and the private enterprise of a gentleman who happens to hold a seat in this House, supporting hon. gentlemen opposite.
How much was spent on that work last year ?
We have not given any estimate yet, but-
There is only a couple hundred dollars, according to the Auditor General's Report-$233.
Since the close of that report, the work has been going on.
Who is the contractor ?
Messrs. Heney & Smith, Ottawa.

How much has been spent since the 30th of June, the time to which the Auditor General's Report carries us ?

The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS ' We have not given an estimate, but I am sure there must be a pretty large amount They are wealthy men, and they are going on with the work.

I find the information given with regard to this work very scanty. We do not know how much has been spent. We only know that we are called upon to spend about $50,000 at a place, that in itself does not appear to be very important- its population being about 350. And we have the statement made and repeated that this work is undertaken to satisfy the political urgings of a gentleman who sits in this House and who is largely interested in lumbering operations in that, distant part of the province. We have the statement of the Minister of Public Works that he has not purchased any site for this wharf. But we have no statement as to the representations that have been made to the department of the need for this work. Have the steamboat companies asked for this wharf ? Have the inhabitants joined together to send in a petition for it? Has anything been shown to the government to make it appear that there is any necessity for it outside the private necessity that has been mentioned two or three times this evening ? It is not fair for the Minister of Public Works to say that he has executed large works elsewhere and that members who happen to come from other provinces, but who take part in the work that it is the duty of us all to perform, that of criticising the government, shall not be allowed to a sic such simple questions as those that I have asked. I can say for my own part, that I think the hon. minister appreciates what I say that it is a pity, if it be true that we are spending such amounts as are provided in this resolution largely, as appears so far in this short discussion, for the private benefit of individuals of some people engaged in lumbering operations when, at present, ns a matter of fact, we have the proof before us since last year at the beginning of the session, that that part of the St. Lawrence navigation whicli interests the people of the province of Quebec so deeply, is absolutely neglected-neglected at least to this extent, that as the Minister of Public Works knows better than anybody else, there is not a sufficient amount spent on that navigation of the St. Lawrence to remove the objections put before the government last year in reference to the dangers of that navigation, in reference to the cost of freights, in reference to cost of insurance. And we have the statement made here tonight, unrebuked, uncontradicted, not disproved by the department, that this large amount of money is being spent to forward the interest of one individual or one company in which a member of this House is largely interested. And we have no statement on the other hand from the Minister
of Public Works, or from other quarters that facts have been brought forward to show need of this wharf or to show that the people of the place demanded it. I know that, in the province of Quebec as elsewhere great pressure is brought to bear upon the government to carry on local works. They are of some use to somebody-nobody will deny that. But can we afford to spend large amounts of money on local works when the general scheme of tlie improvement of the navigation of the St. Lawrence from Montreal to the sea is not being done justice to ?

The improvement of the St. Lawrence is one thing and the erection of the wharf at Grande Vallee is another thing. We are attending to the improvement of the St. Lawrence better than it has ever been done in the past. It is of no use to make so much fuss-for it is fuss that is being made now and nothing else. The hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux) is not in his seat at the moment. He is one of those who came to the government and represented to us that, if there was a wharf built there large lumbering interests would be fostered and developed. We considered the case and came to the conclusion that it was a meritorious work. Now it is not fair and it is not good policy to say that improvements must always be made at places where there is a large population. If by the erection of this woi'k, you help population to settle there, that will be a good thing. Why, we are spending half a million dollars a year to bring population over from the other side.
And wasting a lot of it too.

1 Because this government has thought pro-i per, has thought it was good policy to foster a large industry in that part of the country- a very interesting part of the province and which has vast resources-we are denounced.
1 I say it again, I know the reason ; it is be-| cause the hon. member for Stanstead hap-| pens to have property there. If that non.
; gentleman had not happened to have pjo-perty there, nothing would have been heard ' of tiie matter. But, because an hon. mem! her for this House has lumbering property 5 in that locality, I have done wrong. But ' whether I have done wrong or right-I an r sure I have done-right as usual-the faith \ of the country is pledged, the contract is p signed and I must pay ; there is no escape now. And permit me to add that there ' have been a good many cases worse than ' this. This is not a bad case. Let my hon. ' friends await the developments of the trade I there-they are too impatient. We must 1 give time for the trade to develop which ' this work is intended to promote.

It is the Minister of Pub-r lie WTorks who is making the fuss. I am

not aware that anybody denounced this undertaking or said that it would not foster trade. But the Minister of Public Works has admitted that he has spent this sum of $50,000

Oh, I have no doubt it will be $00,000 before the hon. gentleman gets through. He is spending this money to develop trade. Now, does he not think, when this vast work is being executed purely for the future, that it would be better to erect there a wharf at a cost of $10,000 or of $15,000 and spend the balance to do justice to what seems to me the extremely fair representation made last year by Major Bond, speaking on behalf of the underwriters of Montreal with respect to such general improvements to the navigation of the St. Lawrence either through the Marine Department or through the Public Works Department as to remove from the shoulders of the merchants and exporters of Montreal the heavy burden of the extra premiums they have to pay.

The little money we are spending for the benefit of the trade and of the fishermen in Gaspe will not prevent this country from carrying out the necessary improvements in the St. Lawrence. My hon. friend the leader of a party understands that. The expenditure of $20,000 or $25,000 in Gaspe will not prevent us from carrying out the necessary works in the St. Lawrence. We are attending to the St. Lawrence, and at the same time we are endeavouring to attend to the requirements of the trade and of the population of Gaspe. This is a very interesting part of the country, and great developments are expected by those who are acquainted with it. Now, if we do not show a spirit of progress, if we do not occasionally move in advance of the times, if we do not force progress, we will be accused of being slow. I do not like to be accused of being slow.
I was not present, unfortunately when my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) made his speech against Grande Vallee.
I did not make a speech against Grande Vallee at all.

I may say to my hon. friend that the work at Grande Vallee is a most important one. As a result of this work an improvement is already manifest in that locality. In 1896 when I ran for the first time in that county and visited Grande Vallee, I found that fifty electors resided there. Yesterday I was consulting the census returns, and I found that as a result of this work, the population has increased to 352 souls.
But we only spent up to the 30th of June last, $233 there, according to the Auditor General's Report.

Yes, but the prospective expenditure has already brought to that place a great enterprise. The name of the Messrs. Lovell has been mentioned. They have there perhaps the most extensive lumber mills in the lower portion of the St. Lawrence. The name of the county of Gaspe is frequently mentioned in the estimates. It is true that the government has spent many thousands in that county during the last few years. But we must not forget that there are no railways in the county of Gaspe, that no subsidies have been paid there, and these are the only improvements that have yet been made so far as breakwaters and wharfs are concerned. Now my learned friend speaks of navigation, and the improvements which should be made in the lower portion of the Gulf of St. Lawrence. Prior to 1890 there was no steam communication between Quebec and Montreal, and the different ports and harbours on the coast of Gaspe. As a result of these works at Cape Chat, at Grande Vallee, at Gaspe Basin, at Perce, at Fox river, at Anse a Beaufils. giving facilities and accommodations to the travelling public, a line of steamers has been established between the large centres and the coast. Previous to that period, no steamer would have gone to that coast. But to-day we have several harbours and safe shelters, and as a result, a regular steamship's service. The fishermen of that coast have been treated like slaves for the last century. I have met fishermen on the coast of Gaspe who had not seen a red cent during their whole life. They used to sell their fish to the merchants on the coast and were paid in trade. Since the establishment of that line, and as a result of the improvements which were made by the Department of Public Works, today the fishermen of Gaspe are trading with Montreal and Quebec, and even with the province of Ontario, as Mr. Flavelle, one of the most important merchants and manufacturers of Lindsay, told me a fortnight ago. Therefore, I think my learned friend should not criticise these small amounts, because this is the ' first time since the county of Gaspe has been represented in this House that any grants have been made to it by parliament. The county of Gaspe is the oldest county in the Dominion of Canada.
Is the hon. gentleman talking about other works than this one, or is he confining his remarks to the vote we are now discussing ?

I am speaking of the works which have been constructed at Grande Vallee, at Cape Chat, at Fox river,

at Perce, at Anse a. Beaufils, and at Newport.
What work favourable to steam navigation did my hon. friend refer to as having been executed at Anse it Beaufils ? I thought that was specially for fishermen and not for steamers.
It is for fishermen. At Box river, for instance, a work was constructed last year and the year previous.
At Amherst.

I did not speak of the Magdalen Islands, that is another question. But on the coast of Gaspe, whenever a steamer was caught by a storm, she had to cross the St. Lawrence on the north coast to get shelter. To-day, owing to the works done at Grande Yallee, at Cape Chat and at Fox river, this is avoided. They are most useful works, and nobody would criticise them, on the coast of Gaspe.
Since the hon. gentleman is so well acquainted with that place where there are 350 souls, can he not tell us who owns the land that this dock is to be built on V
Grande Vallee is in a seigniory, and it belongs to the firm of the Messrs. Lovell.
Then this is built on the Lovells' property ?
No, it is built for the general advantage of the people there.
Even if it was.
Well, we would like to own it.
Well, so would I.
I would ask the minister whether, in view of all the information he has with respect to the ownership of this property, he intends to get a deed of the land that will be occupied by this wharf ?

Yes, although I do not believe it is necessary. I have just reproved my chief engineer for having gone on with that work without a deed, but he tells me it is on a rocky point that is not supposed to belong to anybody.
But the hon. member for Gaspe says it belongs to the Messrs. Lovell.
No, the seigniory. This is a shore.

But the less must be included in the greater. Certainly this property belongs to the Lovells. If the minister was building a house for his own use, he would scarcely build it upon another man's property. He would find there would
be some question raised about the title if he wanted to sell the property. Now, I understand this wharf has been built by parliament, therefore it belongs to the country. But we find now it belongs to a company, and the government have been building upon their land. Surely it is the intention of the minister to see that the Messrs. Lovell give a deed. They should make it a free gift to the department.
I do not expect that there will be any trouble as to the ownership but even if there were any trouble we can always expropriate.
There is nothing before us but what has been told us by the hon. member for Gaspe (Mr. Lemieux), that we are expending $60,000 upon a wharf that is being built on the property of Mr. Lovell.
In tidal waters.

If he is the owner of the seigniory he is the owner of the foreshore, If it is on Mr. Lovell's property we would be justified in making this vote conditional upon the government being entitled to a deed of the property.
There will be no trouble as to the ownership of the land.

This is the second instance that has come to our notice to-night in which the title has not been obtained to a property where wharfs are to be erected. I think that the hon. minister should bring his officers up with a pretty sharp turn in connection with this matter, and instruct them that in all cases they shall s$e that no public money is expended on property without obtaining a title to that property.

I have given written instructions which I will bring before the House, to every one of my officers to do in each case, that which has been alluded to here to-night. In the Carnquet case it is a question of $20, and it has been verbally arranged. The deed has not been executed. It has been overlooked. All the same I agree that it should have been arranged because I have had trouble over little things like that. There are certain properties to which we did not obtain titles in the past. I quite agree that we should have titles in every case, and my officers have received positive instructions on that point. They are within hearing of my voice and they know that I have given them the most positive and severe instructions.
That very fact might tend to shake the confidence of the minister in his officers obeying his instructions in other matters.
Oh, no.

The hon. gentleman said that he had given instructions in respect to the purchase of supplies to these officers and that he had absolute confidence that these gentlemen had not exceeded his instructions. In this case he has given just as positive and severe instructions and they have not obeyed his instructions. In this case two new wharfs have been built and in neither case have the title deeds been obtained. I think the hon. gentleman will find that they have neglected his directions in other matters as well as this.
This is a case in which there is much ado about nothing. In one ease there is $20 involved, and you cannot hang a man for $20.
It is not the amount of money.
Where is the big firm in which similar transactions will not happen ? I grant it should have been done.
Where is the big firm that would build on property without getting the title to it ?

There are not many big firms in this country possessing the rights which are conferred upon the hon. Minister of Public Works by the Act respecting the Expropriation of Lands, Chapter 39 of the Revised Statutes, which permits the minister to enter upon and take possession of property for the purpose of constructing public works. All that is necessary for him to do is to deposit his plan, and that plan being deposited, he may proceed with the expropriation. He can do it now, and if he can do it now what is all the row about ?
Yes, but he will have to pay a great deal more for that land if he puts a work upon it before he gets the title.

It is a remarkable statement to say that the Minister of Public Works, after he has entered upon a property to make improvements, as he is authorized by law to do, will be obliged to take into consideration these improvements in the expropriation.
But you will find that a jury will award a much larger amount.
The jury lias nothing to do with it at all. It is the arbitrators who will settle it.
It is the same thing.

When the statement is made that the hon. Minister of Public Works is expending $53,000 in building a pier facing the water front, that the country has no deed for, I will tell the hon. Minister of Justice where all the fuss will come in. In Ontario and in other provinces throughout the Dominion, there are municipalities

and private individuals who own wharfs facing water fronts and I venture to say that these corporations and persons have c;:me to the hon. Minister of Public Works and asked for assistance towards the maintenance of these wharfs, and that the minister has refused to grant them monej. What position is the minister in ? He has told us that he has granted this money without any deed or any claim on the property facing the water front, and he has refused the request that deputations have brought before him, on the ground that the government did not own these properties I say it is a very improper course and it is a course which was not pursued years ago by the government of this country. Heretofore, the government, before they undertook to expend any money on works of that kind, insisted first on the private owners transferring their harbour to the government. This has been the practise in the past, and a proper practise I think. If that practise had been followed out it would not be necessary to impress upon the Minister of Public Works the necessity of building public harbours or piers at these points. To-niglit we have not had a single bit of information as to what will be done at this harbour other than in the general statements made by the hon. member for Gaspfi (Mr. Lemieux), and these statements have reference to five other harbours in addition to this one. If the hon. gentleman had confined his remarks to the subject under discussion the committee could have discussed this matter more intelligently. He should be in a position to tell us the exact condition of affairs at this harbour. He has not given us that information, and therefore we should not pass this item until we do get it.
How much money has already been spent on this wharf ?

The work is going on. We have not yet given any estimate. The two contractors are carrying out their work. Now, while I am on my feet, I may say that in a fortnight I will lay on the Table of the House deeds for these two properties. There is not much in it, but I grant that the property should have been secured by deed beforehand. My officers. I say in their presence, should have done it. It has been overlooked, not because they meant to do wrong, but because they thought it was not necessary. The hon. Minister of Justice tells me that it is better to have the deed and we will have it. At Oaraquet it is a matter of $20 and a verbal arrangement. We will have it in writing.	*

It seems to me that there is something of a disagreement between the hon. Minister of Justice and the hon. Minister of Public "Works. The hon. Minister of Justice informed us a few minutes ago that everything was all right, and if so, he
If Caraquet costs more than $20 then I will pay it.
I am very glad that the hon. gentleman does not propose to follow the suggestion of the Minister of Justice, and that he intends to get the title of that property.
Will the member for Gaspe sa v what is the nearest harbour to Grande Vallee ?
It is about forty miles.
Surely the hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) must have given some good reasons in the first instance as to why this money should be expended.
He has given me the best reasons possible.
What are they ?
The hon. gentleman was not in the House, as he should have been, or he would have heard what I said.
Yes, I was in the House.
I will repeat the useful information I gave before. There are large lumbering operations in sight.
Oh, we heard that.
There was a large increase of population in sight also. If that population increased on the mere hopes of building the wharf what must we expect when the wharf is built ?

It is a very funny matter to spend this $53,000. I can tell the Minister of Public Works that I have been in the House during the whole discussion, and I can say that if all his appropriations are based on the enlightened information he has given to the House in this case, then God help the country. As to the increased population, the member for Gaspe said there were fifty electors in 189G, and that the population
had increased to 350 souls. Will the hon. gentleman multiply the families of the electors in 1896 by the usual rule-
The French rule.
Yes, and I venture to say that he will get 350 souls in 1896. He counted the electors in the one case and the souls in the other. Will he tell us how many souls there were in 1896 V
Did I understand the minister to say that there was a contract for $53,000 1
Yes, signed and sealed.
Who is the contractor ?

Messrs. Heney & Smith, from Ottawa.
Hudson wharf, $1,000.
Have any representations been made to the department as to that wharf not being located where it would be of most use ?

My' chief engineer tells me that we have not received any such representations.
Isle au Coudre-addition to wharf, $6,000.
Is that wharf built at Isle au Coudre for steam boats or sail boats ?

It is for steamboats and for sail boats also.
I am in hopes that Isle au Coudre will become a summer resort of great importance as all the other places on the St. Lawrence are becoming year after year.

The minister says he has hopes, but I do not think it pays the government or anybody else to build wharfs on hopes. If there was any public interest to be served I would like to see a wharf built there, but no steamers go to that place and there is no traffic there at all.

The hon. gentleman is quite mistaken. Steamers stop there. That wharf has been built twenty-five years and we are only adding to it. There is a population on Isle au Coudre of 1,500, and it is increasing rapidly. The climate is fine there. There is a larger number of summer tourists visiting this place than formerly, and there is large fishing and farming interests. Isle au Coudre is one of the most fertile parts of the province of Quebec.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC V RKS.

speechtext: The minister speaks very highly of the island, and I do myself, too. That island has been inhabited for about 250 years and it has a population of about 1,100. If it is such a nice place and such a good place it must have been since last month, because for 250 years it has been growing to a population of 1,100.
They are doing much better now.
Where will the steamer start from and where will she go to Isle au Coudre ?

My hon. friend knows very well that there are steamers starting from Montreal and Quebec, and visiting all these places. This is one of the most thriving parishes of the lower part of the St. Lawrence, and this work is just for the purpose of helping the trade. Two steamers stop there.
Twice a week all summer.

I have been on the boats up and down, and they have never stopped there.
Isle aux Grues-repairs to wharf, $3,500.
I would like to ask the Minister of Public Works again what is the use of a wharf at that island ?

That island is populated by good loyal citizens who want to have communication with other parts of the world, and for that purpose they must have a wharf. They have no railway ; this is an island, and steamers and sailing boats stop at that port. If my hon. friend were located there he would like to have some communication with us.

I believe the Minister of Public Works does not understand exactly the meaning of steamers and steamboats. There never was and there never will be a steamer to stop there;'but steamboats may. I never knew more than .one steamboat, and a small one at that, to leave Quebec in the fall of the year and go there. Many sailboats come from there, but no line of sailboats or steamboats stop there at all.
Where is this removal to take place ?

This vote is intended to help the fishermen to land their boats. If my hon. friend has visited the coast of Gaspe and Bonaventure, he knows that there are rocks carried by the waves and storms, which often prevent the fishermen landing their boats when seeking shelter; and part of this vote will be used to remove the rocks to help the fishermen to land their boats and prevent them being drowned.
I think that is very good, but where are these rocks ?

This vote is a general one, just as we might ask for $10,000 for repairs. Our engineers will report to us that there are rocks to be removed at one place or another. A similar vote is taken every year for the same purpose.

I think the minister himself will see that, small as this sum is, it is a pity that we have not something to show us where the rocks are that are to be removed. Not one of the employees of the department can tell us where there is a demand for the removal of rocks.

My hon. friend is altogether wrong. We could bring more demands than we have money to comply with.
